dossiers.title: Oxford AVT: output accuracy and clinician review

claims: Of 398 logged AVT uses, 37.3% required edits for accuracy.
Recorded reasons included clinical-information accuracy (126), language accuracy (43), and invented information (24).
The report cautions that staff did not always distinguish hallucinations from transcription or templating errors.
Users reported more challenges in complex, qualitative and multi-voice workflows than in structured one-to-one settings.
These are pilot findings, not adjudicated clinical-harm incidents.

dossiers.strengthOfSource: Published real-world NHS pilot with logged use, surveys and interviews; heterogeneous implementation.
knownUnknowns: Original supplier and local risk management file
A particular pre-deployment control decision and version
Clinician review effectiveness for consequential errors
Whether any observed inaccuracy survived authorisation
Specific patient harm or its absence

candidateHazardHypotheses.mechanism: An AVT note may contain inaccurate or invented clinical details that require correction.
candidateHazardHypotheses.potentialHarm: An undetected inaccurate statement could influence downstream care.

candidateHazardHypotheses.mechanism: Variable clinical workflows can alter the error-detection demands placed on clinician review.
candidateHazardHypotheses.potentialHarm: Local review may fail to detect important omissions under particular conditions.

candidateControlQuestions: What reviewed local evidence demonstrates that clinician sign-off detects important inaccuracies in routine practice?
Does that evidence cover the actual consultation complexity, staffing model and model version?
Are downstream record-transfer and post-sign-off error handling addressed?
residualRiskQuestions: Which clinical risk method and version governs the claimed residual risk?
What risk reduction is attributed to clinician review, and on what locally applicable effectiveness evidence?
governanceQuestions: Who owns the local review safeguard and incident-response process?
Who can accept the remaining risk and where is that decision recorded?
dossiers.hindsightBoundary: Reported pilot observations cannot be assumed known to any earlier deployment reviewer; any prospective test incorporating them must be labelled real-world-informed synthetic.

dossiers.title: GOSH multicentre AVT: attribution, negatives and over-summarisation

sourceLocations.section: 5 Interview Data: Accuracy, hallucinations and reliability
claims: Clinician interview themes include fabricated diagnoses, inaccurate clinical impressions and attribution of symptoms or treatments to the wrong source.
The report discusses difficulty retaining explicit negatives, such as absence of symptoms or risk factors.
It also records the importance of proofreading and clinician accountability.
Some participants reported over-summarisation that omitted information regarded as clinically important in descriptive or multi-problem consultations.
The report also discusses positive experiences and benefits rather than uniform failures.

dossiers.strengthOfSource: Published multicentre evaluation with clinician interviews; qualitative findings rather than independently adjudicated incident counts.
knownUnknowns: Incidence denominator for each reported error subtype
Patient outcome for each reported issue
Local control performance in individual participating sites
A specific historic pre-deployment safety decision

candidateHazardHypotheses.mechanism: Patient statements may be represented as a clinician's recommendation or incorrectly attributed.
candidateHazardHypotheses.potentialHarm: Misleading record may influence subsequent clinical decisions.

candidateHazardHypotheses.mechanism: Explicit negatives or context may be omitted through summarisation.
candidateHazardHypotheses.potentialHarm: Downstream clinicians may not see exclusions relevant to clinical risk.

candidateControlQuestions: Is factual and speaker-attribution verification distinguished from simple transcript completeness?
Is review effectiveness tested for negatives and multi-problem or narrative consultations?
Do template configuration and EPR transfer alter safeguards?
residualRiskQuestions: Which errors and remaining uncertainty are accounted for by the local risk argument?
Can evidence from one setting or supplier configuration support another?
governanceQuestions: Who validates the scope and clinical materiality of omitted information?
What review process escalates recurrent misattribution or omission patterns?
dossiers.hindsightBoundary: Interview observations must not be mislabelled as established patient-harm incidents or as information available to previous reviewers.

dossiers.title: HSSIB e-RS: 180-day removal and supplier-deployer controls
dossiers.systemDomain: non-AI referral IT; transferable clinical safety reasoning only

sourceLocations.section: Executive summary; 2.1 The hazard; 2.2 Changing level of risk; 2.4 Summary and learning
claims: HSSIB identified referrals disappearing from worklists, including automatic removal after 180 days without action.
The function was intended to protect worklist performance but also created a patient-safety hazard.
The reviewed national e-RS risk documentation did not mention the 180-day hazard.
Local awareness, documentation and administrative control effectiveness varied, particularly with reduced capacity and unclear responsibility.
HSSIB described provider inability to evidence DCB0160 deployment compliance in the settings reviewed.

dossiers.strengthOfSource: Published national safety investigation interim findings, not an AVT/AI evaluation.
knownUnknowns: Complete original time-stamped decision files for each deploying organisation
Whether a particular reviewer could know the mechanism at that date
Risk ratings, acceptance minutes and local actual control outcomes
Patient-level outcomes for all referrals removed from worklists

candidateHazardHypotheses.mechanism: A worklist performance safeguard can cause pending referrals to disappear from operational visibility.
Local administrative controls may weaken when staffing and responsibility boundaries change.
candidateHazardHypotheses.potentialHarm: Repeated loss of referral monitoring and delayed care.

candidateControlQuestions: Does the organisation reconcile disappearing referrals independently of visible worklists?
Are administrative processes formally implemented, owned and tested under reduced capacity?
Has the supplier communicated the hazard to all relevant deploying organisations?
residualRiskQuestions: Is the competing safety trade-off between worklist performance and referral visibility recognised?
Has residual risk been reviewed when referral volume and waiting times change?
governanceQuestions: Who owns and acts on referral drop-off monitoring and cross-organisation escalation?
Where is local DCB0160 risk assessment documented, and who signs off residual risk?
dossiers.hindsightBoundary: A later investigation finding is not proof the original reviewer could foresee this hazard. Do not infer retrospective negligence or a specific regulatory breach beyond HSSIB's reported findings.
